story.headline: Parmelin to leave Federal Council
story.summary: Federal President Guy Parmelin announced he will step down from the Federal Council on 31 December, opening a seat parliament will fill in December.
story.display_body: Federal President Guy Parmelin announced on Friday 2 October that he will step down from the seven-member Federal Council (Switzerland's collegial national executive) on 31 December, triggering a by-election in parliament. The 66-year-old Vaud winegrower, who heads the economics department (EAER) and is serving his second year as rotating Federal President, said the decision has nothing to do with his health — persistent rumours about his back had circulated for years — and that "no one is irreplaceable" and the moment had come "to make way for fresh forces." Elected in December 2015 as the first French-speaking member of the Swiss People's Party (SVP/UDC) ever to sit on the Council, he leaves after 11 years in which he ran the defence and then the economics portfolios; only this week he defended the negotiated social-partner compromise on wage protection and the EU-CH treaty package in parliament. His departure opens a seat the Federal Assembly will fill in a December vote, with the SVP expected to claim it.
story.why: the resignation reshuffles the federal executive just as parliament is handling the Bilaterals III treaty package with the EU and a tariff dispute with Washington — files Parmelin personally carried — and sets off a succession contest for one of the country's seven top jobs.

story.headline: Up to 900,000 Swiss may switch insurer
story.summary: Deloitte estimated up to 900,000 people in Switzerland will change health insurer as 2027 basic-insurance premiums rise about 5 percent.
story.display_body: Up to 900,000 people in Switzerland are likely to switch health insurer this autumn, the consultancy Deloitte estimated in a survey published Friday 2 October, after basic-insurance premiums were set to rise about 5% in 2027. The estimate — a range of roughly 600,000 to 900,000 — rests on a YouGov poll of 1,236 residents conducted in the third quarter of 2026; nearly half said a premium increase of 20 francs a month would prompt them to consider changing provider, and a quarter reported difficulty paying their premiums at all. The 2027 rise, announced by the Federal Office of Public Health in late September, lifts the average monthly premium to about 412 francs, or roughly 19.70 francs more per month.
story.why: switching insurer is the main lever Swiss households have to blunt a premium rise under the country's mandatory private health-insurance system, so a record churn is less a surprise than a measure of how hard the increases are biting — but it does nothing to change the underlying cost of care.

story.headline: Swiss state pensions rise for 2027
story.summary: The Federal Council raised AVS/AI old-age and disability pensions 1.59 percent for 2027, lifting the minimum monthly pension from 1,260 to 1,280 francs.
story.display_body: The Federal Council decided on Friday 2 October to raise state old-age and disability pensions (AVS/AI) by 1.59% from 1 January 2027, lifting the minimum monthly pension from 1,260 to 1,280 francs. The maximum full pension rises from 2,520 to 2,560 francs, and minimum contributions for the self-employed and non-working also edge up; AVS/AI pensions are adjusted roughly every two years to a "mixed index" blending price and wage growth, and were last changed in 2025.
story.why: the adjustment touches every pensioner and contributor in the country, though at 20 francs a month on the minimum it only partly offsets rising living costs and the 2027 health-premium increase.

story.headline: US sends third carrier toward Iran
story.summary: A US official said the United States is deploying a third aircraft carrier group toward Iran as the US-Israel war on Iran enters its eighth month.
story.display_body: A US official told Al Jazeera on Friday 2 October that the United States is sending a third aircraft carrier strike group toward Iran, as the US-Israel war on Iran enters its eighth month. According to the official, the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier group left its San Diego base on Sunday 28 September, followed a day later by the Makin Island amphibious force carrying more than 2,000 Marines; the official framed the roughly 50,000-troop regional build-up, which also includes F-35 jets, as pressure on Tehran. The claim rests on that single unnamed official and the administration's own characterisation of its intent, which it has repeatedly recast over the course of the war.
story.why: concentrating a third carrier in the region raises the military stakes at a moment both sides say they are weighing escalation against renewed diplomacy, but the stated rationale comes from an administration that has framed earlier moves in this war as "final" before continuing them — so the deployment is clearer than the intention behind it.

story.headline: US delivers first F-16Vs to Taiwan
story.summary: The United States delivered the first two of 66 F-16V Block 70 jets to Taiwan under an 8-billion-dollar sale after months of delay.
story.display_body: The United States delivered the first two F-16V Block 70 fighter jets to Taiwan on Friday 2 October, the island's defence ministry said, as Taipei builds up its forces against the threat of a Chinese attack. The aircraft, built by Lockheed Martin, landed at Chihhang air base in Taitung and are the first of 66 jets under an 8-billion-dollar sale approved during Donald Trump's first term; the handover had been delayed for months, amid repeated requests from Beijing that Washington stop arming the island.
story.why: the delivery is a concrete test of the US commitment to arm Taiwan that Taipei has grown anxious about, and lands days after a Trump-Xi summit at which the two sides floated tariff cuts — underscoring how arms sales and trade now pull in opposite directions.

story.headline: Ethiopia and Eritrea sever ties
story.summary: Ethiopia expelled ten Eritrean diplomats and closed its embassy in Asmara over renewed Tigray fighting; Eritrea reciprocated, unwinding the 2018 peace.
story.display_body: Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations on Thursday 1 October, after Addis Ababa expelled ten Eritrean diplomats and shut its embassy in Asmara, accusing its northern neighbour of "direct and indirect acts of hostility" tied to renewed fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region. Ethiopia's foreign ministry declared the ten diplomats persona non grata and gave them 48 hours to leave; hours later Eritrea called the move "absurd" and said it had "no option but to reciprocate in kind." The rupture unwinds the 2018 rapprochement between the two countries — the peace deal for which Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed won the 2019 Nobel Peace Prize.
story.why: Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a border war that killed tens of thousands, and a formal break between them as the Tigray conflict reignites raises the risk of a wider Horn of Africa war drawing in outside actors.

story.headline: Russian drones shut Kyiv bridges
story.summary: New Russian drone attacks killed at least one person in Kyiv and forced several Dnipro bridges, including the Southern and Paton bridges, to close.
story.display_body: New Russian drone attacks on Kyiv killed at least one person and forced several bridges over the Dnipro River to close on Friday 2 October, the city's authorities said. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Southern (Pivdennyi) Bridge — which carries road traffic and a metro line and had been struck twice in two days — was completely shut, as was the Paton Bridge; Russia's defence ministry said it had targeted a Dnipro bridge used for military purposes. Only eight bridges link Kyiv's western and eastern banks, so closures snarl civilian movement across the capital.
story.why: striking the capital's river crossings widens Russia's campaign against infrastructure as winter approaches, after a brief September truce lapsed and the fighting resumed.

story.headline: Latvia votes amid Russia fears
story.summary: Latvia holds a Saeima parliamentary election on 3 October, with national security and relations with Russia dominating the campaign.
story.display_body: Latvia holds a parliamentary (Saeima) election on Saturday 3 October, with national security and the country's relationship with Russia dominating the campaign. Most leading parties are running on defence pledges after a series of drone incursions into Baltic airspace in recent months; NATO has reinforced the alliance's eastern flank, including German Eurofighter jets stationed about 60 kilometres from Riga.
story.why: the vote is an early read on how Baltic electorates are responding to heightened Russian pressure and the economic cost of cutting remaining ties with Moscow.

story.headline: Fictional worlds train real search agents
story.summary: Training LLM agents with reinforcement learning (RL — learning by trial-and-error against a reward) is bottlenecked by environments: you need tasks with checkable answers, long eno
story.display_body: Training LLM agents with reinforcement learning (RL — learning by trial-and-error against a reward) is bottlenecked by environments: you need tasks with checkable answers, long enough to be interesting, and cheap to generate at scale. The authors build PhantomEnvironments — multi-turn search worlds whose "articles" are generated entirely by templated rules, with no LLM in the loop and zero marginal cost per world — and train agents to answer multi-hop questions by searching that invented corpus.
story.why: the invented worlds share no facts with reality, yet agents trained on them transfer to real-world multi-hop search benchmarks, sometimes beating agents trained on real data — and they learn to scale their search effort with question difficulty. It is a cheap, contamination-free way to make search agents, sidestepping the expensive human-curated or LLM-generated environments the field has leaned on.

story.headline: Protein folding training lifts reasoning
story.summary: Human text usually states answers without the spatial logic behind them, so the authors use protein folding as a teacher: one solved 3D structure yields thousands of exactly-checka
story.display_body: Human text usually states answers without the spatial logic behind them, so the authors use protein folding as a teacher: one solved 3D structure yields thousands of exactly-checkable spatial and topological facts. Their recipe (Fold2Reason) post-trains a model on a protein-folding question-answer set using two signals at once — discrete structural answers through the normal text head, and continuous 3D geometry decoded from the same internal representation.
story.why: besides tripling structure-prediction scores, folding training lifted accuracy on all ten tasks of a broad reasoning suite (spatial, graph, scientific, general), raising the macro-average from 45.1% to 48.3% — concrete evidence that a model can learn reusable reasoning from a hard, checkable physical domain rather than from more text.

story.headline: Switching linear attention rivals softmax
story.summary: Standard softmax attention is expressive but needs a key-value cache (KV-cache — stored context that grows with sequence length), which caps how long a context you can serve
story.display_body: Standard softmax attention is expressive but needs a key-value cache (KV-cache — stored context that grows with sequence length), which caps how long a context you can serve. Linear attention keeps a fixed-size recurrent state instead (constant memory) but is usually weaker. Switching Linear Attention (SwiLA) lets each output dimension pick among several linear-attention components per token, derived as online expectation-maximization over a mixture of linear regressions — adding expressive power while keeping the constant-memory state.
story.why: the KV-cache is the main reason long-context inference gets expensive, so a linear-attention variant that actually competes on recall and language modeling is directly relevant to anyone running long contexts on constrained hardware — an architecture lever, not a wrapper.

story.headline: A stable recipe for recursive reasoning
story.summary: Recursive reasoning models apply one small shared transformer block many times to refine a latent state, buying large effective depth with few parameters — strong on algorithmic pu
story.display_body: Recursive reasoning models apply one small shared transformer block many times to refine a latent state, buying large effective depth with few parameters — strong on algorithmic puzzles and natural as tools an LLM could call. But existing models (HRM, TRM, URM) differ in architecture, gradient handling and training all at once, so nobody knew what mattered. This paper runs them through one controlled pipeline across six algorithmic domains and isolates the variables.
story.why: the recipe for stable, generalizable recursive reasoning turns out to be simple — an intermediate gradient horizon, large physical batches, and controlled updates of the recurrent state — which demystifies a line of work that had a reputation for unstable training. If small callable reasoning modules become part of the agent stack, this is the practical how-to.

story.headline: Measuring if chain-of-thought is honest
story.summary: A chain-of-thought (CoT — the step-by-step text a model emits before answering) is often read as a window into its reasoning, but it can be edited without changing the answer, so i
story.display_body: A chain-of-thought (CoT — the step-by-step text a model emits before answering) is often read as a window into its reasoning, but it can be edited without changing the answer, so it is not always faithful. The authors propose CoT-Interpretability Alignment (CIA), a metric comparing the strategy the CoT describes against the model's internal reasoning as read out by interpretability tools, then try to improve it with post-training rewards.
story.why: across three tasks and three models, agreement was only 44.8–75.9% — a blunt reminder that a plausible CoT is not proof a model reasoned that way, which matters wherever CoT is used for oversight. Post-training on a faithfulness reward raised alignment without hurting accuracy. It extends last edition's CoT-monitor work from a distinct angle — measuring faithfulness rather than gaming a monitor.

story.headline: On-policy warmup speeds agentic RL
story.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR — training on tasks whose answers can be auto-checked) gives agents little signal early, when sparse rewards leave the policy a
story.display_body: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR — training on tasks whose answers can be auto-checked) gives agents little signal early, when sparse rewards leave the policy adrift. On-Policy Warmup (OPW) first trains the student with teacher supervision on the student's own interaction trajectories — including its imperfect actions and recoveries — before switching to RLVR. This was one of several on-policy-distillation papers in the batch, a theme clearly in the water this cycle.
story.why: warming up on states the student actually visits (rather than clean teacher demonstrations) reaches high performance earlier and ends higher than the baselines, and the authors connect it theoretically to trajectory-level distribution matching. It is a practical knob for the expensive, slow early phase of agent training.

story.headline: Looped transformers vary each loop
story.summary: A looped transformer reuses the same layers over and over, and the appealing story is that it learns one algorithm and reruns it each loop
story.display_body: A looped transformer reuses the same layers over and over, and the appealing story is that it learns one algorithm and reruns it each loop. Using graph-walk tasks, the authors show that is not what happens: a single loop can advance by different numbers of steps or stall, so the shared weights are being routed to different operations. They find a learned linear map on the entering hidden state that selects which transition a frozen loop performs.
story.why: it is a clean interpretability result on a trendy architecture — weight-sharing does not mean computation-sharing — and the steering handle (change the hidden state, change the operation) is a concrete lever for controlling latent computation. A caution against reading too much into "the model just repeats its reasoning."

story.headline: Certifying test-time scaling is costly
story.summary: Best-of-k sampling — generate k answers, keep the one a verifier likes most — is reported as a scaling curve of accuracy against k
story.display_body: Best-of-k sampling — generate k answers, keep the one a verifier likes most — is reported as a scaling curve of accuracy against k. The paper's point is statistical: because you pick a compute budget after seeing every point on the curve, you need a confidence band covering all budgets at once, and a naive design to certify 64 budgets to ±1/32 on a 100-question benchmark would need ~192,000 generated answers.
story.why: most of that cost pays for the wrong uncertainty — on a fixed benchmark, about three-quarters of the variance is between questions, which a smarter audit need not re-pay. The authors derive the minimum cost of certifying the whole curve, which is exactly the kind of rigor missing when labs wave test-time-scaling plots around as evidence.

story.headline: Math transfers by method, not topic
story.summary: When choosing math training data, the obvious principle is topic (use probability problems to improve probability)
story.display_body: When choosing math training data, the obvious principle is topic (use probability problems to improve probability). The alternative is reasoning approach (use worked solutions that share a method — say, pigeonhole or double-counting — even across topics). Using two carefully counterbalanced designs where each cell takes a turn as the held-out target, the authors measure which relation produces more transfer after fine-tuning.
story.why: same-approach sources beat same-topic ones in all 40 model–target comparisons across five base models — a clean, actionable data-selection finding (curate by how a problem is solved, not what it's about) with unusually tight experimental controls.

story.headline: Google unveils Gemini 4 Argon
story.summary: The pitch is unusually cyberdefense-first: access starts through Google's "Fairwind" partner program, and Google says Argon (used internally) helped find a critical hospital-system
story.display_body: Google unveils Gemini 4 Argon, its most powerful model — but you can't use it yet. Google announced Gemini 4 Argon on Wednesday 2026-09-30, claiming industry-leading performance in coding, knowledge work and cybersecurity, and released it only to a small group of trusted testers.
story.why: treat the numbers as the vendor's own until independent evals land. Two things stand out anyway — a frontier lab gating a release behind cybersecurity testing rather than shipping broadly, and its explicit bet that chain-of-thought monitoring (watching the model's reasoning and halting it mid-task) is a safety feature worth designing around.

story.summary: Localized editing that genuinely preserves untouched regions has been the weak spot of diffusion image models, so it is the feature to verify once weights ship

The German lab's new image model does localized multi-step editing (changing one region without disturbing the rest), scene composition via bounding boxes and up to ten reference images, and output up to 4K; open weights are promised "in the next few weeks."

story.headline: AI cracks Stratego's best human
story.summary: Stratego is an imperfect-information game (you see where opponents' pieces are but not what they are), with more than a decillion possible setups, games running up to ~2,000 moves,
story.display_body: AI cracks Stratego, one of the last board games where humans still held out. An academic team's system, Ataraxos, beat Pim Niemeijer — four-time world champion and 600-plus weeks the top-ranked player — 15 games to 1 with four draws, and trained on just 16 GPUs for a few thousand dollars.
story.why: this is the kind of milestone the field marks by decades — Deep Blue (1997), AlphaGo (2016) — and it fell not to a hyperscaler's budget but to an academic group for a few thousand dollars, the more striking part. Imperfect-information decision-making under bluffing is the shape of many real strategic problems, from negotiation to security.

story.headline: OpenAI delays IPO over safety
story.summary: The comments land amid a run of hacking episodes involving OpenAI's own agents (including intrusions at Hugging Face and government websites) and a new lawsuit
story.display_body: OpenAI delays its IPO over safety concerns. CEO Sam Altman said the roughly $852-billion company will not go public until it can "make confident safety decisions," speaking at OpenAI's developer day on Tuesday 2026-09-29 as the firm faces fresh scrutiny over agent-security incidents.

story.headline: Judge tosses publisher suits on AI search
story.summary: Mehta — the same judge who earlier found Google violated antitrust law in the DOJ search case — ruled the publishers had only an "expectation" of referral traffic, not an agreement
story.display_body: Judge dismisses publishers' antitrust suits over Google's AI search. US District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed antitrust claims by Chegg and Penske Media (owner of Rolling Stone and Variety) that Google's AI Overviews unlawfully harvested their content and cut their traffic.
